verdict.root_cause: Requests fail inside productcatalogservice's own GetProduct handler. Traces show the error status terminating at the productcatalogservice server-side span for hipstershop.ProductCatalogService/GetProduct and mirroring upward through frontend's client span, frontend's HTTP handler and the loadgenerator parent — the signature of a downstream-originating error [tr_b051a008742f]. The failure is partial (~7-10% of calls, with sibling calls on the same edge succeeding) and carries no latency component: errored spans are single-digit milliseconds, indistinguishable from successful ones [tr_b051a008742f][tr_bd00cef9bc1d]. Every errored GetProduct span contains a successful child call to FeatureFlagService/GetFlag, placing the fault immediately after the flag lookup inside productcatalogservice's own handling [tr_b051a008742f]. The most economical mechanism for a stochastic, fixed-fraction, zero-latency error injected right after a flag read is that a product-catalog failure flag is switched on: the configured value is itself wrong and each request reading it as enabled is deliberately failed. Frontend's aggregate error ratio steps up abruptly at 15:15:30 with no preceding ramp [tr_41bc4b25d0eb], fitting a switch being flipped rather than anything degrading.
verdict.reasoning: Blame sits on productcatalogservice, not frontend, because the deepest errored span is productcatalogservice's own and all other frontend dependency edges — cartservice, adservice, currencyservice, checkoutservice, recommendationservice and the Redis layer — carry spans in the same window with no error status [tr_b051a008742f]. The frontend and loadgenerator alerts at 15:15:45 are the caller noticing. Not dependency_latency: span durations on the failing edge are flat and errored spans are no slower than successful ones [tr_b051a008742f]. Not resource_exhaustion: a fixed-fraction error rate with flat latency and a single abrupt step change rather than a ramp is not the shape of running out of something [tr_41bc4b25d0eb]. Not bad_deploy: an artifact fault would have to fail exactly ~7% of calls at normal speed, and the successful GetFlag child present in every errored span points instead at a value read per-request. The mechanism is the wrong value itself, so the fix is to revert it.
open_questions: The flag's identity and value were never read; the bad_config attribution is inferred from error shape, not observed.
productcatalogservice logs were never retrieved — the Loki selector used a hyphenated name and matched nothing [tr_6fcbf7221788]; a correct-label re-query could confirm or destroy this.

Both change queries ran forward from onset at radius 0 [tr_35bcf24df2ba], so pre-onset changes and any change on featureflagservice or other neighbors remain unexamined; latency, restarts and saturation for productcatalogservice were also never queried [tr_bd00cef9bc1d].

alternatives.root_cause: A pre-onset deployment of productcatalogservice shipped an artifact that errors on a fraction of GetProduct requests.
alternatives.why_not: Unexamined rather than supported — the change window never covered the lead-up — and it explains the per-request flag lookup in every errored span less naturally than a flag-driven injection.

alternatives.root_cause: An unmeasured dependency or datastore behind productcatalogservice returns errors on a fraction of lookups.
alternatives.why_not: The only child span visible in errored traces is GetFlag and it succeeds [tr_b051a008742f]; no failing sub-call was observed, though triage notes one unmeasured edge.

proposal.expected_effect: No action is proposed, so no effect should be observed. The signal that would justify a later action is a named flag/config change on productcatalogservice inside the incident window, plus a productcatalogservice log line under a correct Loki label showing the deliberate-failure path after the GetFlag read; with those in hand, revert_config on productcatalogservice would be expected to drive its error ratio from ~7% (n=20, max ~9.9%) to 0 and frontend's aggregate error ratio back below its ~1.3% baseline within two 2m scrape windows.
proposal.if_wrong: This abstention is wrong if a change-history query run backward from onset (the two existing queries both ran forward from 15:15:45 and returned empty, so the lead-up is unexamined) turns up a productcatalogservice config or flag change with a recorded prior value - that would satisfy revert_config's preconditions and make waiting the costly choice. It is also wrong if a re-query of Loki with the correct label (the hyphenated selector {service="product-catalog-service"} matched nothing, so the logs are unread, not absent) shows an explicit flag-driven failure line. Conversely, if productcatalogservice restart or saturation metrics - never queried - show restarts or memory pressure, the mechanism is process state rather than config and a different action applies. Note also that the verdict's own mechanism is unverified: the flag's identity and value were never read, so bad_config is inferred from error shape alone, and if the flag lives on featureflagservice the right target is not even in the legal blast radius.
proposal.risk: The risk of abstaining is duration: ~7-10% of GetProduct calls keep failing, and every caller of productcatalogservice keeps propagating those errors to loadgenerator-visible HTTP failures for as long as nobody acts. The risk of the alternative - proposing revert_config anyway - is worse and is why I am not: change history for productcatalogservice is empty across the whole queried span, so there is no recorded prior configuration to restore. revert_config would either fail outright or recreate the container with the same values, buying an unnecessary connection reset for all three inbound callers and discarding in-process cache while leaving the flag exactly as it was. Restarting on a config-shaped fault has the same cost and is not reversible.
proposal.blast_radius: Nothing changes, so nobody sees anything new. The parties still seeing the fault are productcatalogservice's inbound callers named in the brief - frontend (and through it loadgenerator's HTTP GETs), checkoutservice, and recommendationservice - at the existing ~7% rate on the GetProduct path. adservice and cartservice edges are clean and unaffected. Had an action been taken, those same three callers would additionally have seen a connection reset during container recreate.

triage_judgement.reasoning: Critical multi-service alerting with frontend and productcatalogservice both seeded within seconds, so this is not a single-service warning or a load-generator artifact. Productcatalogservice is the plausible shared dependency behind the frontend symptom, but the fault class is a prior only.
